utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who has preliminary matters to raise? Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It has to do with witness scheduling and some subpoenas. I'd ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, how long will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Maybe half an hour roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I hope you have had a good rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, will you not, that your memory of all these events was much fresher 14 or 15 years ago rather than today? Is that not a fact, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's exactly same thing. Rather, I think it's true, but when a memory is particularly painful, it never really ceases, does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and could I ask Madam Usher to deliver statements which are already admitted, the statement of this witness from 1994, 17th of January, 1994. And could I ask court usher or court officer in Sarajevo to open tab 1, 2D03-0079. This is the statement for 17th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you see the statement in front of you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We spoke about this yesterday. This has been admitted. You see your own signature right there; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall now go to page 4 in the B/C/S which is page 5 in the English, midway down the page. We'll try to see if we can get something clarified. So this is page 4, line 11. It says: "After half an hour of mistreatment they ordered us not to leave the house, and they walked on towards Meho Aljic's house, which was right next door from the one in which we were staying." Do you see that bit, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And there's a signature, if you look at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, you will agree with me that there is a substantial difference between what you said yesterday in your testimony and what you stated back in 1994 for the purposes of this statement in relation to Meho Aljic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what difference or discrepancy you're talking about. I said that house, that third house and there might have been a house in between. That doesn't mean I said it wasn't far. That's quite sufficient. I don't know if -- that is what I wanted to say. I didn't say that the house was five or ten houses down further down the street. It might have been the third house down -- down the street or the second house. I really can't say exactly, but houses there are detached and that's what I was trying to say. I'm not sure if you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When you said five or ten, do you mean metres or houses further the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not houses. I mean the distance between the houses. It wasn't like one house next to the other. There was some distance between the houses. The houses were detached, you know, the way they were built, and they just couldn't be contiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course I understand that. I have been following your testimony. I followed your testimony yesterday, and I tracked it in this statement, and I think everything that is substantial is identical. I think the 1994 statement is a little more detailed than the evidence you gave yesterday; therefore, I would like to ask you to please go to page 5 in the Bosnian. In the English this is page 6. There. In the B/C/S it's one, two, three four -- line four. In the English this is midway down the page. It's actually marked out. Page 6 marked as page 5, line three. You described what you said here yesterday about Zehra Turjacanin arriving at the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And Emina had brought her there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you just hold on a second so I can ask my question and then you said that she had told you that this, that Milan Lukic was the person who was responsible for that, Milan Lukic and his group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you only mentioned Milan Lukic about that; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not right. I said Mitar Vasiljevic was there too. And Sredoje Lukic was another name that I dropped, but that's after she had been interviewed in Nedici [phoen], sir. I mentioned that yesterday, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that wasn't until after the interview. Thank you for this clarification. It is precisely because of what you just said that I would like to ask you the following question. In this 1994 statement, you mentioned most of the names that you mentioned yesterday during your evidence. You mentioned a number other names that you did not refer to yesterday. You provided a much more detailed explanation back then than you did during your evidence yesterday. May I just be allowed to finish my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sure. Go ahead, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is an eight-page statement that you gave. You signed each and every page of that statement, yet not a word was said in that statement about what you told us yesterday, that you listened in on that interview where you heard Sredoje Lukic's name referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question and the insinuation that -- that the statement's more detailed than your evidence you gave in testimony. If Defence counsel can point to specific areas in the statement where it's more detailed than her testimony, I think that would be more appropriate because I'm looking at the statement and I don't -- and I may -- I'm not sure that I see what -- what counsel is getting at. Moreover, he also said that you named -- mentioned a number of other names that you did not refer to yesterday. So I'd like Defence counsel to put to the witness the other names that he's referring to that she mentioned in her statement which she did not mention yesterday in her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I presume you were coming to a part of your questioning that would be more specific, Mr. Cepic. You're moving from the general to the specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can't leave it at the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And with your leave, my learned friend just stopped me in the middle of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, Vito Raskovic is another name that is mentioned here, another person that you failed to mention yesterday. There are a number of other people, too, mentioned here, but the main thing is not a single word about Sredoje Lukic. You never mentioned his name far back in 1994; right? Not a single mention of Sredoje Lukic's name back then. Isn't that slightly counter-intuitive, madam, especially compared to what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. When I gave the statement, I felt very offended and hurt by Milan Lukic. When I gave that statement I was thinking my husband and about the man who took my husband away. I simply wasn't thinking about Sredoje Lukic or, indeed, Mitar Vasiljevic very much. At the time I was focusing on Milan Lukic. But then at one point, I understood of what had become of those people; those people had been burned alive. There were other families who were suffering just like I was. I felt an urge when I heard about that interview to mention his name too, sir. So there you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I conclude that you weren't interested, back in 1994, in mentioning Sredoje Lukic's name? Is it as simple as that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was filled with strong feelings about Milan Lukic at the time, but I'm just telling you -- I'm telling you what I heard. I can't say I knew Sredoje Lukic if I didn't, and I can't say I knew Mitar Vasiljevic until I heard about Mitar Vasiljevic from my mother-in-law and the other lady that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, is it not ever so slightly strange, perhaps, that you gave this serious statement and you made some serious allegations in it back in 1994 but you said nothing about this, and your recollection was a lot fresher and more vivid about these events in question back at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But my statement is the same. I said exactly the same things that I stated for the benefit of the ICTY. His name is mentioned as it was in all of my statements, but that was after I'd heard about him and not earlier on when I still wasn't aware of him. What I'm trying to do here is tell the truth. I'm not trying to mislead anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what we're after too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, perhaps you are suggesting that I'm lying, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The only information you actually have on Sredoje Lukic originates from Medjedja, summer of 1992, and the fact is you obtained that information as you listened in on an interview provided by Ms. Zehra Turjacanin. That's how I understood your evidence yesterday. You will agree with me that 1994 was two years later, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but when that lady spoke, she was telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We'll be getting to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have statement from 21st November, 1994, and could I ask court officer in Sarajevo to show to witness next tab, 2D03-0077, and could I ask court usher to deliver the copies of this statement in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, do you see this statement? Madam, do you see this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These are your personal details, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry, are we in private session? Could we delete this part of transcript, because we were disclosing details about the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm told it's not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the French booth did mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, 21st of November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was mentioned in the French booth, so court deputy will do the redaction. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, look at the header, please. The 21st of November, 1994, Gorazde centre, your personal details marked on this page. Bottom of page, your signature; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although this looks a little like my signature but this is not a statement that I gave and this is not a statement that I signed, and I have nothing to say about this statement other than the fact that I do not recognise this statement as my own. If you look at page 1, this small sign, like a check, above the letter H. This is not something that I use. I don't write like that. If there is anything at all to this statement, it's certainly nothing to do with my husband or my own fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, I would like to enlist the assistance of a handwriting expert for this. Would you be willing to subject yourself to an examination in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would be perfectly willing to do that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're more than welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, I would not like to waste too much time on this but in this statement you provide a detailed description of some of the things you mentioned yesterday in your evidence. Again Vito Raskovic is a name that we see mentioned here. Hisvan [phoen], Fadila Mujakic, Veljan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Schoolmate Sasa Rosic staying in that room. Everything that you talked about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But do you, for example, see about this staying in the room, sir, with Milan Lukic, what it says about that? It's something that is simply not mine. Do you see that? Do you see that at all? Have you read the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, in detail, very closely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it not a little counter-intuitive that someone would be entering your information, there's a signature that very much resembles yours, someone gives this account about all these things that no one else could possibly have known, yet now you are telling us that you did not author this statement. Is that not just ever so slightly illogical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you see that as something that is counter-intuitive -- well, am I on trial perhaps, actually? Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, I'm merely asking you about one thing I find it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I've answered, haven't I? I have answered that for you. This looks a little like my signature but I simply do not recollect -- recollect ever giving this statement, not at all. I don't remember that full stop. I told you that, didn't I. The first time around when I looked at it last weekend, I went through all of my statements and I went through this one, sir, and that's all I can say about it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, why would anyone try to fabricate allegations as serious as the ones you mentioned in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, that calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. Put in that general frame, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we call court usher to deliver the -- the statements from -- from January and from November 1994 just for comparation of signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, can you please look at your signature. It's right there. You recognise this one as your own. This is the 1994 statement, January 1994. Look at that signature and then look at the signature on the November 1994 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do the two signatures strike you as identical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you it looks a bit like my signature, but if you look very closely --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- you see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the witness be able to finish her answer rather than being interrupted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you had not finished your answer. Did you wish to say something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say this: Your Honour, I do not remember ever making this statement or indeed signing it, although the signature looks like mine, that's true. But there would be no need for me to say this the one time and then all the other times to say something that was different. As I said before, I just wanted to talk about my husband. I wanted to talk about the fact that he was taken away. I wanted to talk about the culprits, the people who did that. Your Honour, nothing more than that. I am here to tell the truth and nothing but truth. I'm here to tell you about my pain and what caused it, and I'm not here to tell you about this gentleman who is just so -- he must understand today, now, that I am a woman sitting here who was wronged. My family was wronged, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- genocide was committed against my family and I'm not here to stand trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam. I have a lot of understanding for all of your pain and suffering during the war and that was my introduction to this cross-examination, was it not? But may we just please have something clarified? If you look at line five, you say: "They took us to Vilina Vlas Hotel. They took us to two separate rooms." November -- the 21st of November, 1994. That's when you made this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 5, you said; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, the 21st of November, 1994, page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Line five. It reads: "They took us to Vilina Vlas Hotel. They took us to --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry I'm a little slow, but at line -- page 13, line 25, he said: "That's when you made this statement." That's a misstatement of what the witness has said, that she said she did not make it statement. I object to that statement made by the -- my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the Chamber has been giving some thought to questioning of this witness on the basis of a statement that she has denied making. You would, of course, be entitled to bring evidence to show that her denial is not credible, but you are not doing that. You are simply putting to her portions of the statement that she has said is not hers. I'm quite prepared to allow you to bring in evidence whether it is independent of her or of any other kind which will go to show that the denial is not credible, but you are not doing that here. You're not succeeding, and we will not allow further cross-examination on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but not along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have tab 3, Exhibit number 2D03-0097, statement given to the OTP from 13 June 2000. And we have in hard copies. Here could I call Madam Usher to deliver.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, do you remember giving this statement to The Hague Tribunal investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could I ask court officer in Sarajevo to show signature on English version of that statement. We just need confirmation on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, these are your signatures on this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: During these interviews you had an opportunity to give the names of all the perpetrators and the victims that you had knowledge about; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but including -- and you also should realise that I gave four statements to different people and on all those occasions I was asked questions in different order and in different manners. So I gave my answers according to the sequence of the questions that were put to me. So if you notice something missing or something extra, that is because of the sequence of my answers given to different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, but we are talking about the same events, about the same perpetrators, and the same victims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only maybe some detail is missing somewhere and some more details are mentioned elsewhere, and this is probably what is confusing you with regard to my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in paragraph 4. Would you be so kind to look at it. And that's line 4, page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entire paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, the one beginning with "Previously." Will you please read that out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just this one sentence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beginning with "Previously"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Previously I gave two statements to the Tribunal, the last --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the answer given by the witness due to the background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of your answer, Witness. I'm going to ask that you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On two occasions I previously gave statement to the Tribunal, and the last one was in the winter of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. The statements that you referred to were given to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And in the course of giving these statements also present -- present were the investigator and the interpreter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, was anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not even my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Where were these interviews conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my home, meaning when I was -- meaning when I was at home and I was a refugee, that is when I gave my first statement to The Hague Tribunal, and then again in a house, but that was my house this time. So every interview was conducted in a house, in Gorazde in the police station there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You said in the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the investigator's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the statements are taken normally. I was in the room where statements were being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The one given in 2000 and signed here, this was given in your home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. Only in 1994 I gave the statement in Gorazde. I just had a baby, and that was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Thank you. During these interviews with the investigators of the Tribunals, these conversations were recorded and certain notes were being made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What do you mean recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statements were taken, and they were noted down on a laptop computer. I don't know about any other recording. So there was just a laptop computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to review your statements and read them before signing them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you signed these statements; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Both this one and the ones you mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were you given copies of all these statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel kindly switch off his microphone. We cannot hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, please see that your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm trying to do that. Your Honours, just for the record we have a problem related to that statements. We never read that statements from OTP. Two statements we never received.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. As we informed Defence counsel in an e-mail before this witness testified, we have done a system-wide search of the OTP and the Tribunal's records and we have not been able to locate any other statements given by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you have heard what the Prosecutor has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, madam, if we look at this statement that you gave in 2000, in paragraph 6 and 7 towards the bottom of the page you talk about your husband being taken away and the incident in the village of Bikavac. You also mention Milan Lukic here and Mitar Vasiljevic in the next paragraph. Therefore, there is no mention of Sredoje Lukic in this statement either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mention Sredoje Lukic when the time comes for me to mention him in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, don't you find it a little bit illogical in the statements that we went through, finishing with the one given in 2000, that you never mentioned Sredoje Lukic in relation to such a major incident? Don't you find it a little bit illogical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said in my statement when I came to Medjedja and while I listened to the interview and her description. I didn't listen her just mentioning Sredoje Lukic and Milan Lukic. I just listened to her description, and I listened to the truth that she was telling in her statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you once again, why didn't you mention that in your earlier statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you. Because I was full of -- I don't know how to put it. I was hurt by the fact that my husband was taken away. I was hurt by what I experienced. I was -- I was obsessed by Milan Lukic. But as years went by, I cooled off a bit, and I realised that this man had committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you testify that this is what you realised more than ten years later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not ten years later, sir. I realised that much sooner. But I think that every statement that I gave, all four of them make sense, if you read them, that is, and they all end in the same way. And the differences can be attributable to the different people who took statements. Some of them didn't ask me about certain things. Some of them wanted to know exactly what happened to me and my husband, how he was taken away and the burning at -- in Bikavac, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, you signed these statements. You confirmed them. You described the incident of your husband being taken away and the one which took place in Bikavac and not once did you mention Sredoje Lukic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection. These questions have been asked and answered, and the statements actually speak for themselves. They've all been admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: One thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would just like clarification where she refers to "this man." It is page 20, line 9, if we could. "I realised that this man had committed a crime." Could you ask counsel to clarify that, who she's referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, to whom are you referring when you say that you realise that this man had committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to Sredoje Lukic. But as soon as I heard Zehra's -- interviews of Zehra Turjacanin, and she spoke in her interview about what was done by Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and Sredoje Lukic, and that's when I realised that Sredoje Lukic was also among those who committed crimes. This is, Your Honour, what I wanted to say. But up until then, I didn't know his name. I had only heard about this being done by Milan Lukic's Eagles, but as soon as I arrived in Medjedja, I personally heard what Zehra told about this whole story.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you mentioned Tasa Hodzic yesterday as being with you on Bikavac on the 27th; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is this a lady of an advanced age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How long did she stay with you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She came that day this happened, that evening. It may have been a day or two all together, but this happened soon after, so the night before -- and that's why she was there and that's why they'd been looking for women from Zupa. One of the girls at the Hasan Veletovac school took a knife and tried to kill. So they were after women from Zupa. That was the reason they were, and that's where Hasa didn't dare say she was from Zupa. That's what she told us, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is my understanding correct, and please set the record straight if I'm wrong, did she come straight to Bikavac from Zupa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. She came from Hasan Veletovac, the school, after that had happened when that girl had attacked one of the Serb soldiers. He tried to rape her, and then she seized his knife and tried to stab him. At least that's what this lady told us when she came. They jumped out the window, whoever, but were still able to escape, and that's how she escaped, and she eventually reached Bikavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions left for you, madam. Please bear with me. Transcript page 2414, yesterday's evidence, towards the bottom of that page you said that Zehra was assisted by a nurse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Bikavac, you mean, assisted by this nurse, or at Okrugla? Do you mean what I said yesterday? What exactly did you have in mind? At Bikavac? She was assisted by a woman they called Hadjinica [phoen]. At Okrugla, the woman who was an employee of the medical station there who therefore must have been nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Right. And that same woman assisted her at Medjedja as well; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other girls who worked at the medical station in Medjedja. There wasn't just a single person. There were several persons who worked there and who provided assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Dressed her wounds and all that at that difficult moment. This is that the nurses did. Is that what you're telling us, and no one but the nurses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Okrugla the first night, I was there myself when they dressed the burns on her forearms and the worms there. The forearms were worm-ridden. I was there myself that first night. I was thinking about applying to actually start working at the medical station, but the night before I just realised that I would not be able to pull it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The same about Medjedja; right? The nurses took it from there, other nurses; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. Whenever I visited her it was always better if she could scratch her head.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just please try to keep your answers brief because I'm about to wrap this up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This wasn't something that was done by any males who happened to be around, just the lady nurses; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but there were men, obviously, who were bringing in the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But the dressing, the wounds were being dressed by those lady nurses; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's at least what I think, because I didn't see any men going about that particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, you explained yesterday and you have explained today that your only source on Sredoje Lukic is the fact that you listened in on Zehra's interview in Medjedja where allegedly she mentioned Sredoje Lukic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I put it to you that Zehra provided several different statements? We heard her live before this Honourable Trial Chamber, as a matter of fact, and we also heard the testimony of the person who medically assisted her at that difficult moment and was there to dress Zehra's wounds, her best friend in those difficult days. There wasn't a single statement, there wasn't a single interview --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection again. He's putting other witness's testimony to this witness to comment on and that's been ruled inappropriate in this Chamber already several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please move on, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: There wasn't a single statement, there wasn't a single shred of evidence, at least as far as your source is concerned, what you claim is your source, your source, and we've seen it all, we've heard it all, not a single mention of Sredoje Lukic's name?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- that's for comment. That's for your final submission to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but -- but the witness testified that the only source was the interview which she heard from Zehra Turjacanin. I have to confront her -- actually, my intention is, if you allow me, to confront her with that source. We have all interviews, we have all statements with Zehra Turjacanin, and I never found the name of Sredoje Lukic, even in testifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. In front of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- interviews we have the statements --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: -- to -- commenting. The witness can hear everything that's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that you wish to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to confront her that statements. Just to confront her all those interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That this was the only source.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That is the source of all the information but we have -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it a question of fact, whether it is the only source, for us to determine?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's for us to determine. Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I just have one question, Your Honour, hopefully in ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, you have testified that at some point you drew the conclusion that Sredoje Lukic was involved in the Bikavac fire. Is that what you've testified to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Other than hearing the name Sredoje, what else if anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic, I thought you were through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that this is a misinterpretation of the testifying of this witness because witness said, I heard from Zehra Turjacanin that he was there, and she confirmed a couple times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It's completely different thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: -- if I have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, from what you heard, did you draw a conclusion for yourself, in your opinion, that Sredoje Lukic was involved in the Bikavac fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You testified that you heard the name Sredoje Lukic from Zehra; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, but it's a question of fact whether she testified. What is the question that you wish to put arising from that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Arising from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was there anything else that you heard Zehra talking about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Be careful now, Ms. -- you haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday that this was a description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. You haven't completed the question, and you cannot lead in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm not leading, Your Honour. I'm asking her if there's anything else she recalls hearing from Zehra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's permissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you answer that question? What else, if anything, did you hear Zehra saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The description that I mentioned yesterday, the description of those men. She was asked during her interview, and then she provided that. She described Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, the hat, the works. And then she described another man who she said was shorter than Milan Lukic, not black hair like Milan Lukic's, rather, brownish, somewhat shorter. Not fat or anything, average really. That was the description, and my inference was this must have been the same person, Sredoje Lukic. That's what I said yesterday, the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: When you say "the same person," you have to give us a name. Can you tell us who you mean when you say "same person"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the reference for this question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It is line -- page 29, line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We already have that answer in the transcript, in line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio. Any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. One moment, Your Honour. Thank you, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence before this Chamber. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal -- well, you haven't actually come, but we thank you for giving your evidence, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much for hearing me out, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution now calls Adem Berberovic, and his evidence will be taken by Ms. Rachel Friedman. Your Honour, prior to the witness being brought in, I'd ask if I could address a quick matter with respect to this witness in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You may sit. And you may begin, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Adem Berberovic, the 12th of July, 1965.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And at that time what village did you live in?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Hamzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What municipality is that in?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Berberovic is a 92 ter witness and I will now proceed to confirm his prior statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, did you give a statement to an ICTY investigator on the 24th of October, 1997?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Will the court usher please call up 65 ter number 65.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, do you see the document before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It's a statement, a witness statement, a statement of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recognise it as your own statement?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When it was originally taken, was it typed in English at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Later, was it read back to you in the Bosnian language and did you then sign the English version?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review this statement in the last few days?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were there any items that you wish to correct in that statement?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: There was a little something, a correction or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I will now ask the e-court usher to hand the witness a piece of paper, a document that I've provided beforehand which -- which is titled "Correction to ICTY witness statement of Adem Berberovic of 24 October 1997." And this document was intended to expedite the confirmation of the statement on the non-controversial issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, do you see the document before you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, completely frankly, I have three years of experience before this court, but I never see similar approach for confirming discrepancy -- discrepancies in a statement such as this one, because my learned friend just put a piece of paper with almost instruction for the witness. For me --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I -- I would agree, Ms. Friedman, that this is an unusual way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We can go -- it's no problem. We can go to each page of the statement. This is based on what was recorded in proofing. It's mostly changes to -- to the way villages are spelled, but I'm happy to go one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say these are non-controversial issues?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: For this trial, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let us look at the first one. Take him through the first one. Let us use that as an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: The first change which is actually found at page 2 of both the Bosnian and English versions, the second paragraph, it indicates the armed -- the unit in which you participated in the spring of 1992. Did you wish to make any change to that, Mr. Berberovic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry, I think maybe it's not clear at this point which column -- I should direct him to look at which column. Maybe if we could call up the statement on the screen, 65 ter number 65. It's there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see now. I'm trying to understand it. I think I understand it now. So in the English statement it's paragraph 2, and as recorded there is a reference to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the correction is the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I can ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask the witness if that's the correction that he wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, is that the correction that you wanted to make, from the "Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina," to "The Territorial Defence"?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at the next item, it's at the second page of both the Bosnian and English versions, the fifth paragraph. There is a name of the place beginning with a C. Mr. Witness, what was the correction you wanted to make to the name of the place from Crncima?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What is the correction you wanted to make to the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Crnca, Crnca. There's a C with a check right above it instead of just an ordinary C.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Next at the fourth page, second paragraph, you refer to a man by the name of Mitar. Do you now wish to indicate the last name of this person named Mitar?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, on page 6 -- sorry, on page 5 in the Bosnian version, third paragraph, which is the fourth paragraph of page 5 in the English version, there is a reference to a soldier named Vitomir Raskovic. Do you wish to correct that name?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what would that correction be?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Vitomir Rackovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now on page 6, the Bosnian version, second paragraph, and that's third paragraph in the English. There's a place identified as Pozarcici. What is the name --

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Pozarcici.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 6 in the Bosnian version, third paragraph. This corresponds to the fourth paragraph in the English. There is a reference to a detainee at the Uzamnica camp named Nurko Dervisagic. You wished to change his name and what would -- as you indicated, and what would you wish that change to reflect?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Nurko Dervisevic, Dervisevic not Dervisagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Next on page 9 of the Bosnian statement, fourth line, and this is in the fourth paragraph in the English statement. There is a reference to a man called Sekeric. Did you wish to change his name?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sekaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Also on page 9 in the fourth paragraph, which is the last paragraph in the English statement, you have confirmed that the first of the four young men referred to is not last name Sisic but, rather, what?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Finally, one change which was not on the original document I provided. In that same paragraph it states: "Ten or 15 days later, Lukic took out both Bajic, 17 years old, and Nermin." You have stated that you wanted to make a change to that sentence or to that idea.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Who was --

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Instead of Bajic, there was Nermin, Karic and Nermin, the two of them instead of Bajic. It's not Karic and Bajic, rather its Karic and Nermin.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us briefly what happened to Mirzo Bajic if he was not taken on that day?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Bajic stayed with us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what eventually happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic came and killed him later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: With those corrections do you confirm that the statement you made on the 24th of October, 1997, is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It has been a long time, that much is true. One forgets a thing or two, but I still remember everything that I stated back then, and if I were to provide another statement it would be identical to this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender the statement of Mr. Berberovic into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P142.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, how did you come to know Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I hadn't known them before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think this is a leading question. That is my humble opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Both men are referred to in the statement that has just been admitted into evidence of Mr. Berberovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On that basis it's not leading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, you began to answer but it's not recorded. Could you please tell us how you came to know Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I met them upon the arrival in the barracks, in the camps where we were. That is where I met them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure did I hear in B/C/S plural or single, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's it. That's it. I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Which barracks or camp are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: The Uzamnica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the first time you met them?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: We were in the camp, in the hangar. That's where we stayed the whole time. And one day they came to the hangar. The guard opened the door for them, and they started beating us. They beat me as well. Dervisevic, (redacted), Kustura as well. Hajrudin Ahmedspahic too, Hasan Balic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did any of the men that beat you say anything to you or to anyone in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Lukic told me, "Fuck your Ustasha mother. You have green eyes like a true Ustasha."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How long was this after you arrived at Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean how long?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: The first time that they came to beat you, how long was that? An approximation is okay. How long was that after you arrived at the Uzamnica barracks?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Ten or 15 days after my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And how did you know the two of the men that were beating you were Milan and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know immediately. Nurko Dervisevic, however, did know. And when they left I asked Nurko Dervisevic who are these men, and Nurko told me who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What did he say to describe who Milan Lukic was?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I asked him, "Who is this dark-haired man," and he said it was Milan Lukic. And the one with the brown hair, he said, "That is Sredoje Lukic." There was also Milos Lukic who had kind of blonde hair. His name was Milos Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How did Nurko know who they were?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He knew because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. This is calling for speculation. We cannot have the sources in that way. We already have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able to lay --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did Nurko tell you how he knew these men?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll allow that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He knew them because he had come to the camp two months before me, and they used to come to beat him even before I came there. Saban Murat was also with him and he knew Milan Lukic as well because they went to school together, and that's what Saban told him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at page 38, line 17, the witness actually mentioned the name of a protected witness. If we could have that redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did Nurko tell you anything in particular about the relationship between Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is again the same objection. In my previous cross-examination, Prosecutor objected for the -- almost the same kind of questions, and it was not allowed to me, if I remember, if I jog my memory. So I think that they're not proper questions. That's my humble opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: The question does not suggest any answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, more properly you could have asked, Did Nurko tell you anything about Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I can ask it that way, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, did Nurko tell you anything about Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I asked him who these men were, he identified each one of them, and I asked him, "How do you know?" And he said, "Of course I know, because they had come here before and they beat me and maltreated me." There were only two of them, Dervisevic and Saban Muratovic there when I was brought.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberovic. You testified that these beatings happened in the hangar. Can you describe what the lighting was like?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: There was no electricity, and if you opened the gates there was light coming into the hangar, but it was not enough as it would be the case with a proper lighting, but there was visibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When this incident took place, what time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It was sometime around noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When they came inside the hangar, was the door left open or shut?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It was open.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were you able to see the men clearly?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What was the distance between you and them?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Not more than five or six metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And after that day when you were told who they were, were you able to recognise them on your own?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you come to recognise their voices?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, I think we have to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Groome. I have to say that in the absence of Judge David, Judge Van Den Wyngaert and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, something has arisen that required -- makes it unable for Ms. Friedman to complete her examination. She asked me to extend her apology to the Chamber. And if it's acceptable to the Chamber, I'll complete the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I had an experience like that when I was prosecuting years and years ago, but I had to take over -- yes, I had to take over from somebody. Yes, that's -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, can I ask you how often did you see Milan Lukic at the camp during the time that you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the time that you were detained at Uzamnica, approximately how many times did you see Milan Lukic there?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Many times I saw him, because he used to come often to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate how many times per week or per month?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He would come every other day or every three -- once in three days, then he would not come for a while, then he would appear again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How often did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He beat me with his feet, with his boots, with his fists. Once he brought an electric baton and told me to come to the centre of the hall and to bend down. Then he started beating me with this baton on the back. However, the -- it fell down, and he started cursing my balija mother and accusing me of having cost him 500 marks for this baton. That is what he paid for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You have just testified "it fell down." What are you referring to when you say "it"?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: The inner segment fell down from -- from the baton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what you recall about this baton?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It was in the shape of a police baton, a truncheon, but as soon as he started beating me these inner segments or elements started falling out of the baton. He put his hand on his head, cursed my balija mother, and told me that I destroyed -- or that I caused damage of 100 -- of 500 marks, which was the amount that he had paid for this baton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you at any time have physical possession of this baton?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you understand him to mean that you had broken the baton?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he probably thought that he destroyed it because of me, because he came to beat me. I didn't invite him to come to beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where precisely did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: In the barracks in Uzamnica where we were, in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What time of day did it occur?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Afternoon, around 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall if the door to the hangar was open or shut?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Open.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate the distance between yourself and Milan Lukic during this event?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It was close. He told me to come into the centre of the hall and to bend down, and he was standing next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have any -- were you able to see him clearly?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate how many times altogether you were beaten by the person you describe as Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He came many times to beat me. When we were taken to perform forced labour in Ugljari, if he happened to pass by he would drop by and beat me there as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone in front of him, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've mentioned a place that you were taken to for forced -- what you described as forced labour. Could I ask you to, once again, tell us the name of the place you were taken.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It was called Gornja Mahala and Cadzava. There was a restaurant there. Next to the Cadzava was a sort of a warehouse and this is where we unloaded wheat and other stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic ever beat you outside of Uzamnica camp?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: When we were sent to the neighbourhood of Okolista to perform forced labour. This is where their command was. We were forced to unload coal and to take out slag from the boiler house, et cetera. And we were asked to come out and have lunch, but not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I might ask you --

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: -- only after five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could ask you a specific question. You said: "This is where their command was." Who is -- who are you referring to when you say "their command"? Whose command was it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: The command of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate during -- over the course of your detention, when did this particular event occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Okolista doing the work that you have described, did you see Milan Lukic at any time?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe the circumstances under which you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: You mean in Okolista, to the command if I saw him or are you referring to some other place?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm asking you if at the command in Okolista if you saw Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No. Only once. I saw him when he beat me with a wooden bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were you when he beat you with a wooden bat?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I was in the kitchen. This man took us to have lunch after we finished work, and as soon as we got in, he came into the kitchen with this wooden baton. He told me to move away from the other man two or three metres and to bend down and he started beating me with this bat. This bat broke into pieces he beat me so fiercely. He went away and brought another bat and continued beating me. I was covered in blood. I lost consciousness, and later on I don't remember anything else. When I came round, they poured some water on me. I looked around, but he was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, so the record is clear, who is the "he" that you're referring to that hit you with the bat at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic ever address you by a particular name?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to Sredoje Lukic. Approximately how often did you see him at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understood this witness testifying under the Rule 92 ter and we already have a statement of this witness. Actually, statements, two statements given to the investigators of OTP. And I'm a little bit confused now. Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I was going to ask the same question. It's really nullifying the purpose of 92 ter if the examination is going to be so lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are just about ten more questions that I wish to put to the witness, and although we may have gone over the half hour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to make up your mind whether the witness is 92 ter or going to be viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many times did you see Sredoje Lukic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I used to see him because he also came to beat us and maltreat us. That was his only purpose, just to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever -- were you ever present when Milan Lukic had a conversation with Sredoje Lukic with respect to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave I think that we have already all those questions in the statements. I don't see the purpose of this examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You seem to be just reiterating what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the particular piece of evidence I am seeking to elicit now is not in the statement, Your Honour, and again I will try to bring the examination to a close as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you present when Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic had a conversation with respect to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that this question is leading question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think you have to reformulate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll go back to my original formulation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you ever prevent when Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic had a conversation with respect to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's still leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's still leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And we have answer of witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's for us to determine what weight to attach to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the time that you were detained at Uzamnica, did you ever see Sredoje Lukic outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I used to see him in town when we went to the Red Cross to unload humanitarian aid. We went also to the utility company to dig trenches for the water company if there was any leakage or breakage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe for the Chamber what, if any, injuries you sustained or permanent injuries you sustained as a result of your detention in Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I have suffered the following consequences: I lost sight in one eye. I cannot sleep. I have headaches. I have pain in my arms. I have pains in my back, in my spine, and I have pains in my left leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look around the courtroom to see whether you recognise anyone, but before I do that I want to ask you, do you need to wear any glasses to -- to see the people here in the courtroom clearly?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now we have Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave just for the record usual objection for that kind of identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Alarid too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Both objections are noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
