utterances.text: Once you put on your glasses, I'd ask you to carefully look around the courtroom, and if you do recognise someone to please indicate that to us.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I recognise this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to indicate where the person you're -- you recognise to be Sredoje Lukic is in the courtroom by indicating where they are sitting in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is quite unusual --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- cannot -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- but just for the record direction which witness shown is in direction of my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm seeking to ask him to describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We can have a video record, so I kindly ask that portion of the video is exhibited. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The person that you say you recognise as Sredoje Lukic, can you describe where they are sitting in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And with your leave, I think that witness said [B/C/S spoken] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] How is that translated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Interpreters note the witness only said, "I cannot."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: There is nothing in the transcript. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear what the witness -- just don't say anything. Don't say anything. If you go to line -- what is it, line 6 -- 50, number 6. After Mr. Cepic said: "It is quite unusual but just for the record direction which witness shown is," and then you said something, Witness. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those two over there, Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. That's them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let -- Mr. -- you need to curb your proclivity to rise, Mr. Cepic. Let the Prosecutor complete and then you can have your say. Let's see what you can make of this, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, you've just said on the record, "Those two over there, Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. That's them." I want to ask you specifically for -- to -- with respect to each person individually. Milan Lukic, do you recognise the person that you know as Milan Lukic in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to indicate to us? We cannot see when you point who you're referring to, so can I ask you to take a close look at the person you believe to be Milan Lukic and describe what that person is wearing for us.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: A black jacket. He's the man on the left next to this gentleman in a blue shirt. Right next to him is Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The person you're referring to as Milan Lukic, can you see the colour of his shirt or any other article of clothing that he's wearing?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Some sort of a blueish shirt and a black sort of jacket or something. One hundred per cent certain it's Milan. Milan Lukic, 100 per cent. Sredoje is right next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The person that you're identifying as Sredoje, can I ask you to describe what he is wearing from what you can see from where you are sitting?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: A jacket, black, I think, and a shirt, blueish, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you see any other article of clothing that he's wearing?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: The thing -- black. I know. I know it's them. One hundred per cent certain, no question about that. Milan Lukic first, second Sredoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe which person is Milan Lukic with respect -- the relationship between the two people? You keep pointing with your hand, but can you tell us with respect to using directions left and right where they are in relation to each other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I really apologise for interrupting, Your Honour, but I think that I haven't heard the name of Sredoje which is filed on 52nd page, line -- line 5, second. He just said second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sure I heard him say Sredoje, second Sredoje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters confirm that that is indeed what they heard, second Sredoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, using the directions left and right, can you describe where these two men are in relation to each other?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sure. It depends on where they're seated or where your perspective is. Black hair. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to -- to do it from your perspective. So as you look at them do it from your perspective using the directions left and right.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: On the left Milan Lukic, on the right Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that the witness has identified Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm not so confident that witness from his position identify correct sides as Mr. Groome said. That is the first -- first I would like to address. Secondly, if we -- if we could have opportunity just to, after the sessions of course, listen to one more time the tape and check one portion of -- of testimony. That is the technical issue, of course, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What portion do you wish to have checked, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The first part of identification, Your Honour. I already objected that, but just if I have opportunity with technical service to do that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I haven't ruled on that. I'm not sure I understand the request. You want to have the tape played in relation to the first part of the -- Mr. Groome's questioning on identification? Is that what you're requesting? If so, why?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I already -- I already pointed that the some part of testimony of this witness missing. You addressed that. Page 50, line 6. And I would like to do that after the sessions, maybe tomorrow, next day of tomorrow during the next week. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: I'm sorry -- I think that was word that you thought was missing but we learned through the interpreters that he had identified -- oh, sorry, that he had identified the right side. It was a word that you thought was missing but the interpreters, when Judge Robinson asked, confirmed that they had used the -- the expression on the right side. That's how I understand it. But you didn't have your headphones on so you didn't capture what the interpreters clarified, so I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Just to check one more time. I'm little bit confused, to be completely frank. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: You can do that from the transcript if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to compare transcript with video recording. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Yes. You're always free to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise for interrupting the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just in a similar vein, Your Honour, my case manager indicated to me that she felt that there was a mistake or a word that was not used at page 51, line 12, and we thought we heard -- she -- I can't tell instead of "yes." And that -- so we would, of course, make the same reference to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there is a procedure in place that's just simply a matter of filling out a form and reporters will go back and re-listen to the tape and we certainly won't question them if they -- if they recheck the tape and make some change to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Whatever the procedure is you will follow it. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm assuming it's my turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Berberovic.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My name is Jason Alarid and I represent Milan Lukic and I'd like to ask you a few questions. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in anticipation for your testimony today, you reviewed statements that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's the 1997 statement. But you also gave a statement in the year 2000; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave a statement in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you also gave a statement to the Association of Women Victims of War the 7th of July, 2008, this year, this summer, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But do you also recall the 6th of November, 1994, giving a statement in Sarajevo to the security -- state security services?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: A statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't give any statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could the court usher please bring on the screen 1D10-2903 which is the B/C/S version and 1D10-2895 which is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you -- are you able to read the -- the Bosnian statement at the top or do we need to make it full screen for you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: This is quite blurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But it is -- it is true that your -- your birthday is the 12th of July, 1965; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your birth date is not the 7th July -- excuse me, July 12th, 1965?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat what he just said? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you please repeat what you just said? The interpreter didn't hear. Perhaps you should come a little closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree with this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your birth date?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: The date of birth. You knew that before, before this statement. Somebody [as interpreted] could have put it right there and somebody could have typed this up, but it wasn't me who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you had a point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yeah. Witness -- thank you, Your Honour. 22nd line, it is not somebody could. You could have put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody could have. Somebody could have written the date of birth and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the court usher please go to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: My signature. Yes, this is my signature, but I didn't make this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you please go to page 2, please, bottom of the page. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Page 3, bottom of the page. Is that your signature as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me tell you one thing. It is my signature, but the statement is not mine. I gave a statement there, back home, and the date that is reflected here, I never made a statement on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: And are you could have typed up whatever you liked, but this is not my statement. The signature is though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could -- could we go --

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we go to page 4, please, bottom of the page. Is that your signature as well, sir? Actually, I think that's the next page. I believe that's page 5.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, my signature, but the statement is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we go to page 6, please? Okay. Sure. Next page. Is that your signature as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But -- now, you -- did -- are you saying that you spoke -- or is it true that you spoke to members of your security services in Sarajevo at some time in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I did speak to them, but I don't agree with the date. Not on that date. The date does not tally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Are you saying the 6th of November, 1994, that doesn't refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: After I'd been exchanged, in the period right after, I did not make any statements. So I'm telling you I did not make this statement on this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When -- when did you make the statement?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Not before 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you sign a statement in Sarajevo in 1995 and maybe that there was a mistake or a typographical error at the top of this page? And first page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I did sign the statement that I made, but this doesn't tally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you recall the statement being approximately seven pages?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just in terms of some background information, you joined the Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that was in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know when the war began. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so in April of 1992 is -- is my understanding of when the -- or -- as a matter of fact, let me just ask you the question. When about the Uzice Corps come to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: In April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that on the 19th of May the Uzice Corps withdrew from Visegrad? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that the Uzice Corps burned Dobrun to the ground? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at some point in time in May of 1992, the Uzice Corps surrounded your village and then six Chetniks came into the village asking for weapons and licenses; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And during that time period some people gave their weapons up to these soldiers. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then later those same people were arrested and taken away by the Uzice Corps; correct? And then they were released later.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Some were released and some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it was at that point in time that you discovered that some of those people that were taken away had been beaten by the Uzice Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: They were taken away to the Visegrad MUP, M-U-P, and that was where they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And they were interrogated by police there or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is it true that on the 19th of May, 1992, is when you believe the Uzice Corps left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why do you remember that date with such certainty?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Because I know when they came, and I know when they left, and I know how long they spent there. The 19th of May. I know exactly that that was the day they left Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I'm looking -- and so you know, sir, I am looking at the English translation of this statement that we just looked at your signatures at the bottom of each page, and so I'm asking you if these things are true so you can verify maybe if there was simply a mistake of when you gave the statement but not that you didn't give the statement at all, okay?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I know that it wasn't on that date. I see the date and the date is just not right. The signature, yes, it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your statement it's translated that after the Uzice Corps left Visegrad that's when the White Eagles entered the town and started to torch houses and kill the remaining Muslims. Is that fair -- is that -- would that represent what you would have stated in a statement?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was the White Eagles. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, other witnesses have testified that when the Uzice Corps first came to Visegrad many Muslims were rounded up and taken to the football stadium. Do you remember that or did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It's not that I heard of that. I was there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And so were you there when Colonel Jovanovic came in in a helicopter and landed with a lot of fanfare in front of all the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And were you there when he addressed the Muslims in that stadium?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He addressed them and then he lied to those people there, lied to them. He said they should go back, work their land, don't be afraid. No harm will come to you. And then the people went back, but then the killing and the throat slitting started. Therefore, he had lied to those people there. I'm sorry, sir, that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And -- and what -- what has been testified before in this -- in this courtroom is that Colonel Jovanovic said that if the Muslims didn't comply with him that he had control of the White Eagles. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I know he told people to go back to their homes, to till their land, to sow the seeds, to go to work, that they would not be as much as touched by anyone, but it wasn't the truth he was telling them because people went back to their homes and then they started killing everyone. Everybody was working their land, digging up, and ended up killed. They killed all of them. He actually lied to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, after the Uzice Corps left you were -- you were defending your people, a member of the Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter didn't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, sir? The interpreter didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My question was that after the Uzice Corps left, you still were defending your people as a member of the Territorial Defence. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had guards behind the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you would often stand watch with binoculars; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it was at that time that at 500 metres or so distance you saw an individual kill a woman and two children and throw them into the Drina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, according to the statement that I'm looking at, there was no date of this. Can you tell me approximately when that happened, in June, May, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: That happened in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you realised that later in 2000, November, you gave a statement identifying that person as Mitar Vasiljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you didn't mention that in either your 1994 statement nor your first statement to the ICTY in October of 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I said in my statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What I was saying, sir, is you didn't mention Mitar Vasiljevic's name before November of 2000 in a statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't do it before. Depending on the sequence of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- but when exactly were you captured?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at the time you were a soldier; correct? You were fighting in the conflict in August of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you were a member of the Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any weapons at the time. We took women and children across Crni Vrh towards Medjedja and Gorazde. You can ask anyone and they will confirm that I didn't have any weapons. You can ask your people over there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were captured by approximately 12 Chetniks in camouflage and olive-grey uniforms; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in those groups you recognised Milos Tantalic; correct? And Vito Raskovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vito Rackovic, not Raskovic, Rackovic. He used to work with me and I know him by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that these men took you and beat you severely, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you describe that for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I can. Milos Pantelic hit me in the stomach with a rifle butt, then they took me by my hands and started dragging me along a road covered in gravel. I was screaming from pain because my -- my leg was hurting. They took a ground sheet and put me there and took me to Gornja Lijeska to a room where a shop used to be before the war. They started maltreated me -- maltreating me and beating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- and isn't it true that it was the same group of men that had captured you that continued this beating? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These men were there as well, but there were others who were at Gornja Lijeska. There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- well, in your statement to the ICTY, October 24, 1997, the number of men that -- that now beat you in this room had grown to 50 soldiers. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you didn't mention that many in 1994. You were only mentioning the names such as Vito Rackovic and Milos Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I can tell you that it was when they found me there in this field. There were Serbian soldiers there. But when they took me to Gornja Lijeska there were guards there and there were some other soldiers as well. The room was packed with men. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And these gentlemen, they -- they tore all your clothes off, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milos Pantelic did that. He took a knife and cut all my clothes, leaving me only in my underwear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then they took you to the police station. They took you to the SUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That night when they beat me up -- or, rather in the morning Milos Pantelic and his brother Uros Pantelic came, told me to get ready and to choose which bridge they would take me to throw me over, and I said, "I don't care. We can go either to the old or the new bridge." Milos Pantelic also told me to get ready, but I asked me [as interpreted], "What am I supposed to put on, since you have cut all my clothes? He hit me and said, "Who tore your clothes?" And I said, "It was you." So he and his brother Uros took me out, put me into the military carrier. They tied my arms -- my hands and my legs with a wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- and isn't it true that those -- Milos and Uros were police officers, weren't they, in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms were these people wearing that first captured you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is it true that at that time you were wounded by a gun as well?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: They set an ambush for us when we were escorting the civilians to Medjedja, and this is where I was wounded. They started shooting from the ambush, and that is how I got wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's the same day you were captured or was that much earlier?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: That was during the night while we were escorting the civilians, and on our way back we ran into the ambush. The people dispersed. Some went to Crni Vrh, and some went in other direction. I was found in the morning when the dawn broke, and that is when they took me to Gornja Lijeska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And after you were untied from that armoured vehicle, the person that untied you kicked you to the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then a policeman took the keys to the car and it was a policeman that transported you to the Uzamnica barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it was on that first day that you got there that you were -- you arrived severely wounded and beaten, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the only two people that were there was Saban and Nurko; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in fact later -- or isn't it true that it's your testimony that Nurko didn't know Milan Lukic but only learned that from Saban; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Nurko told me, but -- and later Saban told me as well, but Nurko was the first one to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Nurko told you that Saban told him that it was Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Saban knew him. Nurko didn't know him. Saban knew him because they went to school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, according to the statement from 1994, there's an indication that that's when you believe Milan Lukic came to the Uzamnica barracks just the second day after your arrival. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't come the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at that point in time isn't it true that, according to your statement in 1994, Milan only kicked you one time in the chest?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He kicked me in the chest, and he went on to beat other men. He didn't beat me again on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then according to the 1994 statement, Milan came the next day; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then isn't it true that he didn't come until seven days after that? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, he came regularly, every two or three days. Then he would not appear for a certain period of time, and then he would start coming again. That's how it was. It's impossible for me to record every single day. Maybe I should have kept a diary or took notes, but I had no paper or pencil to write down the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But isn't it true that according to your 1994 statement, you only mentioned a total of four times that Milan Lukic came to the Uzamnica barracks? And then you mention one time --

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I said that Sredoje Lukic came four times, and Milan Lukic came on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then in your 1994 statement you go on to say that Milan Lukic came once when you were shoveling coal, and that's what you testified here today as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true, though, that in your 1994 statement you indicated that Rade Milosavljevic -- Milosavljevic beat you every day?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would take me out in the evening, in the small hours of the night. He used to take me out, and he knocked out two of my teeth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And according to your 1994 statement, the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 was the worst part of your detention; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you identified in your statement other members that beat you part of the daily beatings; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: You will have to repeat this, what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you identified other guards or members at the barracks that beat you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I know who beat me, and I didn't mention other guards. I just gave the names of those who beat me. But guards changed. There were rotations. One would come, the others would go away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that at a certain point in time the beatings stopped at Uzamnica barracks?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that was after the warden changed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not because the warden -- actually, it was because the warden sent the guards to the front line. He immediately sent them away the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And these were the barred -- the guards that used to beat you daily; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would tender into evidence the 6 November 1994 statements as earlier referenced as 1D10-2895 as the English version, and 1D10-2903 as the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit 1D61.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in your statements you indicate that Milan Lukic had black hair; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what colour would you say your hair is? Would you say it's brown, dark brown, or black?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I ask you to look at the gentleman that you identified as Milan Lukic, and I put to you that isn't it true that his hair is lighter than yours?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Whose hair is lighter than mine?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The person whom you identified as Milan Lukic. Can you look at him again?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic is the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true his hair is lighter than yours? It's not black.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't care. It's irrelevant now. I know the man. I am 100 per cent sure that it's him. I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Are there any distinguishing features on this man that you met at Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How tall was he?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He was rather tall but not too much. He's not short either. Middle height. He was neither fat nor thin. He was a young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In centimetres can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a metre in the camp to measure him. I can't give you any rough estimates now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did he have any features on his face, any birthmarks or moles?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't take a good look, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was he -- did his uniform have short sleeves or long sleeves?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: It depended on what the weather was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you notice any tattoos?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He had a green uniform, winter uniform -- or, rather, camouflage uniform. It was green and white, and it had snowflakes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you ever notice any tattoos?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when was the last time you believe you saw Milan Lukic? Can you give me a month and a year?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: When a new warden of the camp came, I didn't see him again after that in Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you remember when the new warden came?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to remember. There were three or four of them in a sequence. This one was in 1993 or 1994. I think 1994. When the new warden came he stopped coming up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so is it your testimony that Milan Lukic was able to come to the camp the entire year of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't come every day. Yes, he came throughout the whole year of 1993, but not every day. As I said before, sometimes two or three days would elapse and then he would come, then he would be absent for a certain period of time, then he would appear again, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are you including the first part of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so basically you're saying that Milan Lukic did not come after January 1st, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He didn't come up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you estimate how many times Milan Lukic came during 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: More than ten?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: More than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Which months?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Each month in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were released the 6th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how long were you forced to shovel coal?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't digging coal. I was unloading coal and slag from the boiler house. We took the slag out of the boiler house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how long were you in the Kula prison in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Me? I was never there. Kula in Sarajevo? Oh, we spent one night there. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: That was prior to our exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Immediately prior to your exchange? When was that?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: We were at Kula in the evening, and women and elderly people were exchanged first, and some young men as well. Nurko Dervisevic and I were left as well as one man from Rogatica, and we were exchanged sometime around 7.00 in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And was Saban also there in Kula?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at this time, Your Honour -- actually, no. I tendered the statement I wanted to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Berberovic.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My name is Jens Dieckmann, and I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Sredoje Lukic. I have a couple of questions for you, and I will put them to you as short and precisely as possible, and I would highly appreciate if you could answer my questions in the same manner, just short and precisely if it's possible for you. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: First and foremost I want to offer you condolences of my client and for the whole team for all the suffer you gone through through the last years.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: If you do not understand the question, please indicate it immediately and I will try to rephrase my question and you could try to answer again. Mr. Berberovic, in the time of the Uzamnica camp, you were detained together with Nurko Dervisevic. That's true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many months you have been together in Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: From August 1992 until the 6th of October --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness repeat the year, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could you tell us the year?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1994, until we were exchanged. So from August 1992, the 15th of August, 1992, until 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. As far as I understood, we are still in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we in private session? No, we are not in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I would like to go in private session just for some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you were together with all of them in one hangar during your time of detention in Uzamnica, the one hangar?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was with them in one hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So if there was any mistreatment in the hangar, it would have been observed by all the other detainees, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we -- could we call up the statement from November 1994? This is 1D61. To page 4 in the English version. To the fourth para, and page 4, para 5 in the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sir, in this statement you described in this paras in front of you, this is para 5 in the B/C/S version, you describe mistreatments. Is it true that Nuro [sic] Dervisevic was present during this incident that you describe there in this incident?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You describe mistreatments, and I ask you if Nurka Dervisevic -- Nurko Dervisevic was present during these mistreatments that you described there done by Milan Lukic and his group.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. In the hangar, but we used to go out and do some work. And we weren't together while working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Friedman -- not Mr. Friedman. Mr. Dieckmann, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, due to your memory you and Nurko Dervisevic were beaten on more than one occasion by Sredoje Lukic. This is your statement, true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we go in private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we call up the document P142, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, I want to show you again the statement from the 24th October 1997. I would like to go to page 9, para 5 of the English version. And it is page 9, para 2 of the B/C/S version. Okay. Thank you. I just want to read out some sentences to you. "I was beaten by Milan Lukic and his soldiers many times. He came quite often to the hangars, about every two or three days. He beat me in the hangars. He never took me out of the hangars. He and his soldiers would just enter the hangar." This is your statement from 1997, and you stand by by the statement today?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: They would go into the hangar and beat us. They didn't just go in and stand there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: But they never took you out of the hangar for the mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we please call up the document which is released under 2D03-0181.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This is a statement, Mr. Berberovic, you have given on the 7th November 2000 to the ICTY. If you could just see -- you have both statements on your screen, the English and the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And if you see on the left side of the screen you see your name and your birthday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: That is the birthday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we in the English version please go to page number 4. And could we show page number 4 of the English version, please, to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This is your signature under the statement from the 7/11/2000? Is it true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: What date is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: 7th November 2000.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I made a statement in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Correct. But there's a second statement from the ICTY from the 7th November 2000. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we please go to one page before, the page number 3 in the English version. And this is page number 4 in the B/C/S version. I'm sorry, page number 3 also in the B/C/S version. And I refer to the very last paragraph on this page at the bottom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, I will read you the English version. "You have showed me a photo spread with 12 photos of men. Picture 3 is Sredoje Lukic; 7 is Milan Lukic; and 9 is Mitar Vasiljevic, but he looks older than I remember him and he has no moustache." So could you remember that a photo spread has been shown to you during this -- during this interview? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Photos were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Right. Correct. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sir, you have confirmed that this is your signature under the statement from the 7 November 2000. Isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And by signing the statement you confirmed that the statement contain the truth and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear the question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Should I clarify my question again?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: No need.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could it be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 2D20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave just for the record, we have asked several times for photospreads to the Prosecution and we never received once, so we are not able to confront the witness with these photospreads mentioned in this statement, and we want just to put it on the record for the procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was an issue that came up repeatedly in our 65 ter conferences. While the Prosecution was able to produce some of the photospreads, some were missing. We -- I initiated an extensive and exhaustive investigation into some -- the photospreads that were missing, and unfortunately there are some that have never been found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, speaking for myself, I'm quite alarmed at that. It's very important, very vital evidence that really ought to be available to the Defence, particularly in a case where identification is -- is the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And as is clear from the 65 ter Conference, I, too, am shocked and expressed my shock and dismay and had -- and had an extensive inquiry done into the matter and had people search boxes out at the beach building and every possible conceivable place where these photospreads could be. I don't believe there's any other thing else that I can have done to locate them. I believe that in the switch -- or in the attempt to archive the Vasiljevic case that they were inadvertently shredded by someone, and I fully appreciate that their absence is something that may very well be considered against the Prosecution in its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll certainly consider that, Mr. Groome. Yes, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, as far as I have understood your testimony, you did not know Sredoje Lukic prior to 1992. Is it a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could you please describe Sredoje Lukic due to your memory? What is his -- his height?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Can he please [as interpreted] stand up so I can get a good look? I -- I know which one he is when I look at him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said which one was which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour, because my learned friend doesn't speak B/C/S. If I intervene just in the transcript. The word "please" did not use. It is -- thank you. Page 81st, line 18.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Cepic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 81st page, line -- line 18. It is without "please." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, you're being asked to tell us your recollection of Sredoje Lukic's height. So the intention is that you would tell us, unassisted by the Accused Lukic standing. So are you able to do that, to tell us what is your recollection of his approximate height?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm able to tell you, sir. He was a man of medium height, on the plump side. Rather short than tall. Shortish. He wasn't tall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Lukic was taller than him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you give us informations about his age? What was his age as you remember?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what his age was. When he started coming over there, he looked 30-ish, 35 possibly. I'm not sure if my assessment was quite accurate at the time of his age. I'm really not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: If you say that -- that Milan Lukic is taller than Sredoje Lukic, due to your memory is it -- is it perhaps 20 centimetre, the difference between both?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He is taller than Sredoje, taller. How much taller exactly it's difficult to say. Maybe 15 centimetres, maybe 20. I wasn't taking measurements. He was taller, that much I can say. Now you're asking me about centimetres. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. All right. Sir, in line 22 you're saying, "He is taller than Sredoje." Which person do you mean with "he is taller than Sredoje"?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Berberovic, you told us here on page 67, line 1, that you didn't -- that Nurko Dervisevic told you that he didn't know Sredoje Lukic before his time in Uzamnica. Mr. Berberovic, do you know that Nurko Dervisevic had known Sredoje Lukic for 15 years prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: But did you know that Nurko Dervisevic has been detained in Uzamnica from June 1992 to October 1994, which totals 28 months?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He was taken prisoner on the 9th of June, 1992, and exchanged the same time as me in 1994. The 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Do you know that Nurko Dervisevic has lost two of his sons during the war, killed by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He told me that his two sons had been taken away. That's what he told me. I didn't see it. He had two -- he had twins, two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sir, you described frequent times mistreatments of Sredoje Lukic against you and others in Uzamnica. Would you change your mind today if I tell you that Nurko Dervisevic testified that he has allegedly seen Sredoje Lukic only on one occasion during the whole period of his 28 months imprisonment in the Uzamnica camp? Only on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe he didn't see well, whereas I had good eyesight. He came. I saw him four or five times. I don't know about Nurko and how many times he saw him. I don't know how he could possibly now not have seen him because he was together with me in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sir, would it change your mind if I tell you that Nurko Dervisevic told in his testimony that he was alone in -- on this one occasion when Sredoje Lukic allegedly mistreated him and not in presence of you or other prisoners? I refer to page 1963, line 5 to 7 of the transcript. Could you give me an answer, sir? Could you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: What question? I'm sorry, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Would you change your mind if you'd be aware what Nurko Dervisevic told us here about his allegedly mistreatments he suffered?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Do you know any reason why Nurko Dervisevic, who lost two sons and who, according to his own testimony, suffered in consequence of his time in imprisonment should lie here in the Tribunal? Do you know any reason for this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know how many times he came. I mean, Sredoje Lukic. What Nurko said and what he said about how many times he came, I'm not interested in that. I know how many times I saw him, and he was telling what he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, I put it to you that your testimony today, as well as your prior statements, are wrong as far as Sredoje Lukic is concerned. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I understand you well, but I'm not mistaken. What you claim to -- to be my wrong opinion, it's -- it's not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berberovic. I would like to change the topic. Mr. Berberovic, on the 15th of August, 1992, you told us you were captured by the Serbian army. True?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And since the beginning of June 1992, you have been a mobilised soldier of the Muslim army, true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I was in the Territorial Defence, TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Since you served in the labour platoon which was located in the Abid Kreso's house in Hamici village, you could hear and learn details of all plans and operations which were being prepared in the area by the Muslim commanders Ahmed Zejdic [phoen], Himzo Vilic [phoen], Nezija Mezic [phoen], and Zakib Kakar [phoen]. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. First of all, I wasn't in the army as you put it. How can I be in army if I didn't have a rifle? I wasn't a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could we call up the document 2D03-0143, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This is a statement -- minutes given to the Ministry of Interior, public security station in Visegrad, on the 20th of August, 1992, and I would -- I would ask the court usher, please, to go to the -- to the bottom of this statement. At the bottom. Mr. Berberovic, could you identify your signature on the left side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I remember this statement, and it's good that you showed it to me. I like this statement. I like this statement being shown to me. That suits me. And now you want me to say something about this statement. I had been forced to tell any kind of things what was necessary and what was not necessary. Sorry, you asked me to explain. Shall I tell it to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. First of all, I just wanted to know if this is your signature on the left side on the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I wrote this under coercion, under duress.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So first of all, you confirm that this is your signature and that this statement has been given on the 20th of August, 1992? You could confirm this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I did make a statement but under coercion, because Lazar Drasko forced me to do that. He was a Judge before the war, and Radmila, I don't know her last name, I forgot, she had blonde hair, she was limping, and these two forced me to sign this and to tell all kinds of things, the things that I knew nothing about and the things that I knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Please, sorry, I want to say what I want to say. Excuse me, now that you have raised this question --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What else do you want to tell us about the circumstances under which you say you were coerced to make this statement, because the Chamber's interested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Mr. Lazar Drasko forced me. He was a judge before the war, and he's still a judge in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did he force you? How did he force you to make this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He forced me to tell him what I knew about and what I didn't know about. I told him I -- there are things that I know nothing about, but he told me, "You must remember." And then he took a pistol and hit me on the head with the butt and I started bleeding. He repeated again that I had to admit and to confess. After that, the lady judge, Radmila, stood up. I don't know her last name, but she was a judge as well. She stood up and pulled me by the hair and slammed my head on the desk and told me that I must tell them and remember everything, and that is how under the duress I was forced to sign this statement. That was in the barracks in Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So it is not -- your statement, it is not true that this statement was taken by Mr. Vukica, Veselin Vukica?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was there in the office with us. Veselin Vucelja [as interpreted]. He used to be a schoolteacher before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: With the leave the Chamber I would like to confront the witness the contents of this statement and ask him if he remembers that he has given this statement and if this statement is true or not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean the very statement that he said was made under duress?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Because as far as I have understood him, he did not say that it was -- that he did not give informations. So he gave informations, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But if the Chamber accepts that he gave the statement under duress, surely this statement is worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, I'm not saying that the Chamber has made up its mind. I'm saying that if we accept that the statement was made under duress, then it's of no value. I think your line of attack would be to challenge his allegation that it was made under duress.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sir, just -- just one -- one question to -- to this statement. Isn't true that you have been captured during combat activities in the area of the Koracim village? Have you been participated in combat activities before your arrest? I'm sorry, the Kocarim village.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in the army. You can ask anyone you want. A man without a weapon cannot go into combat. This was not a combat one-on-one. We were taking the civilians to the other side, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that in this statement the judge you mentioned is never mentioned neither in the statement nor as someone who signed the statement? Isn't it true that he was not there, the judge you mentioned? Mr. Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Judge Draskovic and this woman, this female judge was there, and there was a recording clerk as well. That's how she introduced herself and said that she came from Belgrade, and she typed this. And Radmila and Lazar Draskovic were judges. And also to Muharem Samardzic. And he hit me with a pistol on the head and my head started bleeding, and Radmila took me by the hair and slammed my head against the desk and they forced me to sign it. I'm not going to repeat this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, could you give us a reason why they started these procedures against you? What was the reason to force you to give a statement like this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: That's a good question. Mrs. Radmila, the judge, told me to make a statement and that after that she wouldn't know to what prison sentence I would be sentenced, but she said that I would definitely spend my life in prison. So in other words, one could interpret that to be a death sentence. But I don't know what was their intention with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Isn't it striking to you or isn't it perhaps illogical that somebody who never had a weapon and was just an ordinary man is put under such a pressure by judges like this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: This was obvious. Ask anyone. They will tell you. Whoever has no weapon is no soldier. If I didn't have any weapons on me, I wasn't a soldier. I only tried to save my wife and my two children, sir. Sorry. And my old mother. She was 65 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sir, did you give -- did you give information to them or did they present you this statement just to sign? Does this -- I'm sorry. Yes, perhaps -- please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: They asked me to start telling them what I knew and what I didn't know. I told them what I knew. After that, they forced me to keep talking about things that I knew nothing about. They also forced me to say that even if somebody had no weapons that they did have weapons. How is it possible? How can I do that? How could I say that someone had weapons if they didn't? Probably they had some of their loved ones killed and now they wanted to force me who killed this person, and I couldn't tell them that, and for that reason he hit me on the head with the pistol and this female judge pulled my hair and banged my head on the desk. I cannot confess to anything that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: But how could you provide interesting information if you were not in the army in any important level or department of the army?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I know what I was doing. I know what I said. I was in the kitchen. I was chopping wood for the kitchen. That's what I was doing. And that is because I was unarmed, and I wasn't in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sir, would you say that this statement in front of you does not reflect any factual information that this is true? Or is -- or does this statement contain information that is in fact true and reflects your experience?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't care about this statement. This statement was made under duress. I was coerced into telling them what they wanted to hear. Either that or I'd be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would -- I would ask for admission and to tender into evidence of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour. The Prosecution would object. Very few of our rules consist of a single sentence but Rule 95 is one that does consist of a single sentence and it says: "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." I submit that this statement is such a document. Even if the Chamber has reserved its views with respect to what the witness says were the circumstances surrounding the taking of the statement, on its face it was taken during the course of -- of over two years of an illegal incarceration of this -- of this witness. I think there's an invariably strong inference that it was not taken under circumstances which were anything less than coercive and I think that the Chamber must reject it in compliance with Rule 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, in your jurisdiction when a statement like this is challenged as to its admissibility, let us say a confession, before a ruling is made isn't there a voir dire, a trial within a trial, to determine whether this statement was made under duress?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In -- yes, Your Honour. In the jurisdiction that I practised in it would actually be done before trial because it's deemed so -- such a matter of critical importance, and there would be a separate hearing to -- to adjudicate the voluntariness of a statement, and depending on what was decided by the judge in -- after that hearing, if it were suppressed, there could be no mention of it at a trial and it would not be admitted in evidence under any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, are you saying here that we have sufficient information to make that determination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe by the very fact that the date on the statement is in the middle of a -- of an illegal incarceration that lasted in excess of two years is sufficient for the Chamber just on that, without having to even evaluate whether -- what this witness says about having his head slammed into a table and having a pistol -- being struck over the head with a pistol, without even having to evaluate that, I believe the date of the statement and the fact that it occurred during his incarceration is -- is sufficient evidence for which this Chamber should just summarily reject this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear Mr. Dieckmann in reply now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to confess that we were not aware about the alleged circumstances of the production of this evidence, and for our -- due to our opinion it is quite important for our defence, and it is of probative value and relevance because of the possible motives and motivations of this witness, how to testify today and in earlier statements, and therefore, we -- we called up this statement, and therefore, we think that it should be admitted into evidence. And it is quite obvious that this is a statement from 20 -- August 1992 and not from a later position. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: But, Mr. Dieckmann, isn't it sufficient for you to make the point that you want to make as you have done and for it to be on the record? Why would we need to have the statement which we -- by its very nature and the way in which it has been obtained is unreliable and probably inadmissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, due to our opinion, it's -- it's finally a question of -- of weight of this statement, due to our opinion, because in confrontation with the statement, of course, the witness made his statements and give his comments about the circumstances, but there -- his -- his comments about it. And on the other hand, there are detailed informations in the context of the situation, it has been five days after his -- his arrest, and we -- we think that this -- that this statement is admissible under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann. The Chamber has listened to the submissions on both sides. The Chamber finds that the witness is a witness of truth in relation to this matter. The Chamber accepts his evidence that he gave this statement under duress. As such, it is valueless following Rule 95. It will not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, finally, I would like to go to the statement you have given to the Association of Women Victims of War in July 2008. You have given this statement, don't you? You remember this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this statement primarily concerns the matter which I had raised earlier that I'd asked that it be taken in private session. If it's going to -- if Mr. Dieckmann is going to deal with that matter, I'd ask that we go into private session to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you're going to deal with the matter that Mr. Groome mentioned earlier, then it will be private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: We could into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Berberovic, the last question that Mr. Dieckmann asked you was about whether or not Mr. Dervisevic had a problem with his eyes, and you said yes, he had problems. Can I ask you to simply explain what was the problem with his eyes?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: He complained about not being able to see properly and that he probably needed to wear glasses, but there was no possibility for him to obtain a pair of glasses. Circumstances were such that he couldn't get glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just use this opportunity maybe one question additional question for this witness and his problem with sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This witness, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what is the size of the glasses that you wear?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is the size of the glasses that you wear?

utterances.speaker: ADEM BERBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I got these glasses in another country, not in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I noticed that you had problems with your sight when you entered the courtroom. You would agree with me that Mr. Nurko Dervisevic has better sight than you do, won't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're really getting too far, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I don't know about that, what kind of dioptric glass he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer. Don't answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions and I do have a brief matter I'd like to raise with the Chamber before the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be as brief as I can. Next week the Prosecution is scheduled to call a retired member of the Serbian government to testify. Earlier -- or during today's court session we all received a letter from the Serbian government requesting -- making certain requests. I would like to acknowledge the great assistance the Serbian government has been in this matter with respect to this retired member of one of its services. I've spoken during the break with my colleagues on the Defence, and they would have no objection to certain protective measures. So if the Chamber is willing to entertain an oral application with respect to certain protective measures with respect to this witness, I'm prepared to make that in less than a minute and perhaps we could avoid having to file written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They're requesting, Your Honour, that his identity be protected. So I would -- the Prosecution would seek that he be given a pseudonym, and the next available pseudonym would be VG-142 according to the numbering system that we've used in the course of this trial, and I believe also facial distortion would be appropriate. They have expressed a concern about certain aspects of his testimony might reveal his work as well as his identity. I believe those can be appropriately dealt with by going into closed session where necessary. So although they are requesting that the entire evidence be taken in closed session, I don't believe that's necessary to protect their -- their concern. So the Prosecution would just be asking that he be given -- assigned the pseudonym VG-142 and that he be granted facial distortion, and we will take care to go into private session where consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, any views on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We have no objection to protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll grant the application for pseudonym and facial distortion for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I might just remind the Chamber with respect to the subpoena for 24. I received another e-mail a few minutes ago. They're waiting in Sarajevo just to have some guidance about the -- from the Chamber with respect to what the interpretation of the Chamber's subpoena should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will express its opinion shortly. Tomorrow, do you have witnesses for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. None for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we've filed the schedule. There are no witnesses. Some witnesses are arriving -- the witnesses we have for next week arrive, I believe, Tuesday and Wednesday. So the Prosecution would only be able to produce witnesses on Wednesday and Thursday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Wednesday and Thursday. So we will adjourn now and resume on Wednesday ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the parties to be ready at short notice to be in court tomorrow at 2.15 in the event that the Chamber is in a position to announce some decisions, but you'll be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We're adjourned.
